# leibler

> leibler (leibler.dev, from Kullback-Leibler) is a data lab that helps companies own their intelligence. It post-trains a specialised model on the company's proprietary data and on synthetic data that matches its real-world tasks, so the model beats the frontier on speed, cost and accuracy for that company's work. The models are built by Kullback, leibler's open source agent. On the example agent on the home page, measured against GPT-6 Sol at one million tickets a month, the trained model costs one tenth as much, has one twentieth the latency and is 35 percent more accurate.

Frontier models are trained for everyone, because serving everyone is how frontier labs make their revenue. A company's agent does one thing, the same task a million times a month, and needs depth, not breadth. A post-trained 9B to 27B model is 10 to 100 times smaller than the frontier, so it runs on cheaper GPUs, handles more traffic and replies faster. The customer never touches a GPU.

## How it works

1. Describe: the customer types the behavior they want (for example: on a broken item, ask whether a replacement works before offering a refund). Kullback writes eval tasks for it, each with context (who the user is, their ID and email), requirements (the database rows the agent must change) and judges (did the agent do this, did it do that).
2. Ground: Kullback connects the customer's traces, business knowledge graph and request, and, with permission, their GitHub and agent harness, so the synthetic environment matches production.
3. Build the environment: from a week of traces it builds data (the records the runs touched, with the values they saw), tools (one function per tool, behaving the way the real one did in the logs), rules (the customer's policy, turned into checks that run before every write), a simulated user who knows only what the real one knew, and one verifier per task that looks at the final data and says pass or fail. Every value points back to the line in the trace it came from.
4. Review: Kullback writes the eval and the training data. Every eval case and training example is a file the customer can read. Reject one and Kullback rewrites it.
5. Evaluate: Kullback runs every model on the eval cases and grades it on what it changed. The bar is a score the customer sets.
6. Train: if no model clears the bar, Kullback generates training data for the same eval scenarios and post-trains the customer's model with reinforcement learning until it clears the bar.
7. Host: leibler deploys the model, routes a small share of traffic to it first (5 percent in the example) and rolls out fully when it holds for 24 hours.
8. Watch: Kullback re-runs the eval whenever a new frontier model ships and tells the customer if anything changes.

## Key facts

- The customer's data stays the customer's. Training runs on the customer's workflow and never leaves the customer's account. The model is the customer's to download or host anywhere.
- Kullback runs as three agents taking turns until the environment holds and a model clears the bar: the Builder, the Examiner and the Writer.
- The runner is frozen only after a person confirms it, and every verdict carries the hash of the environment and the runner it ran on.
- Worked example on the home page: an online furniture shop runs a support agent on its inbox, in four steps (email arrives; look up the customer and check the order exists; read the situation, so a loyal customer gets an instant refund and anyone else is offered a replacement first; draft the reply), one million times a month. On a frontier model it costs $48,000 a month, takes 4.0 s per reply and scores 64 of 100 on the shop's tickets. The trained model, refund-v1, costs $4,800 a month, takes 0.2 s per reply and scores 86 of 100.
- How to start: bring one workflow. leibler evaluates it against the frontier for free. Evaluation in 48 hours, a hosted model in about a week.
- Open source: Kullback (https://github.com/leiblerdev/kullback) is Apache-2.0. Pull requests are welcome; the maintainer reviews every one. Its environments are on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/leibler).
- Founder: Krrish Agarwalla (krrish@leibler.dev). Krrish researches post-training models for chip design with Dr. Amin Arbabian at Stanford, and mathematical reasoning with Dr. Hinrich Schütze at LMU Munich. The method comes from the research.

## Glossary

- Trace: the logs the customer's agent already writes; Kullback's input.
- Environment: the rebuilt system the agent worked in, made of data, tools, rules, a simulated user and a verifier per task.
- Verifier: one per task; it looks at the final data and says pass or fail.
- The bar: the score a model must reach on the customer's eval before it is hosted.
- Builder: the Kullback agent that rebuilds the system the customer's agent worked in from its traces: data, tools, rules, user.
- Examiner: the Kullback agent that writes a verifier per task, probes the build, and sends findings back to the Builder.
- Writer: the Kullback agent that turns runs that pass into eval cases and training examples the customer can read.

## Questions

- Q: What is leibler? A: leibler (Kullback-Leibler) is a data lab that helps you own your intelligence. We post-train a model on your proprietary data and on synthetic data that matches your real tasks, so it beats the frontier on speed, cost and accuracy for your work.
- Q: Why not just use a frontier model? A: Frontier models are trained to be general, because serving everyone is how frontier labs make their revenue. A model post-trained on your workflow is more accurate on it. It's also 10 to 100 times smaller, so it costs less, runs on cheaper GPUs, handles more traffic and replies faster.
- Q: What is Kullback? A: Kullback is the open source agent behind leibler. You type the behavior you want and it writes eval tasks for it, with context, requirements and judges. It then generates training data for those scenarios and post-trains a model with reinforcement learning. The code is on GitHub under Apache-2.0.
- Q: Why trust synthetic data? A: Kullback builds a synthetic environment from your traces, your business knowledge graph, your request and, with permission, your GitHub and agent harness, so it matches production. Three agents, the Builder, the Examiner and the Writer, then take turns, hardening every task and checking it with its own verifier before it's used.
- Q: How big is the model? A: Typically 9B to 27B parameters. In the example on this page, a 9B model beats the frontier on the shop's own tickets.
- Q: Does my data leave my account? A: No. Training runs on your workflow and never leaves your account. The model is yours to download or host anywhere.
- Q: Do I need GPUs or an ML team? A: No. You tell Kullback how your agent should behave. It writes the eval and the training data, trains, hosts, and keeps watching the frontier. You never touch a GPU.
- Q: How does it compare with a frontier model? A: In the refund email example on this page, the trained model refund-v1 costs $4,800 a month against $48,000 for GPT-6 Sol, replies in 0.2 s instead of 4.0 s, and scores 86 of 100 instead of 64 on the shop's tickets.
- Q: How long does it take? A: Bring one workflow. leibler evaluates it against the frontier for free. Evaluation in 48 hours, a hosted model in about a week.
- Q: Who is behind leibler? A: Krrish Agarwalla, who researches post-training models for chip design at Stanford and mathematical reasoning at LMU Munich.
